presenceNote: c.1715 is the earliest dated Shawnee site in Kentucky (Eskippakithiki); 1795 is the Treaty of Greenville. The general area claimed or used (most of present Kentucky, drawn as the whole state outline as the most generous estimate) is approximate, low-medium confidence and NOT a boundary: no source gives a line. Ohio towns are a county footprint, not a boundary.
overlapNote: Overlaps Cherokee (treaty lines 1768–1775), the Six Nations (who ceded Kentucky to the Crown at Fort Stanwix 1768 over Shawnee objection), Chickasaw (far west) and Delaware, Mingo, Wyandot and Miami in Ohio. Sources disagree on which Kentucky claim was strongest (see the Cherokee file). The Ohio River line of 1774 is a colonial understanding, and its terms are not preserved.
basis: General area: West Virginia Encyclopedia (“most of Kentucky”) and Henderson 1992 (“claimed much of it”), drawn as the Kentucky outline; no boundary is sourced. Hand-simplified from Greenville (1795) and Fort Finney (1786) treaty text, secondary accounts of Camp Charlotte (1774), and site evidence (Lower Shawneetown, Eskippakithiki). Native Land Digital data was not used.

eras.text: General area claimed or used by the Shawnee, c.1715–1795: approximate, not a boundary, low-medium confidence. The West Virginia Encyclopedia says the Shawnee “consistently claimed” the hunting lands west of the Alleghenies “along with most of Kentucky”, and Henderson (1992) says they “claimed much of” the region while the Cherokee and others used parts of it with their permission. No source gives a boundary, so the map shades the whole present outline of Kentucky as the most generous estimate: effectively most of Kentucky, not a surveyed line. The c.1715 start is the earliest dated Shawnee site in Kentucky, Eskippakithiki (Clark County, c.1715/1718–c.1754); Lower Shawneetown at the Scioto mouth (mid-1730s–1758, about 1,200 people in 1751) is the second. The sources do not date when the claim began, so c.1715 is a use date, not a claim date. Main villages and summer camps were north of the Ohio; small winter camps lay south of it until the 1770s.

eras.text: After Lord Dunmore’s War, the Shawnee agreed at Camp Charlotte on Scippo Creek, Pickaway County, Ohio (19 Oct 1774) to stop hunting south of the Ohio and to recognise the river as the boundary. No copy of the treaty survives, so the terms are known only from accounts. The claim to Kentucky did not simply end: Henderson notes it was still contested in 1775, and Shawnee attacks on Kentucky stations continued through 1782 (West Virginia Encyclopedia). The general area (still the Kentucky outline, now a lighter dashed tint) is therefore shown to 1795, approximate and not a boundary. The line drawn is the Ohio River from the Kanawha mouth to Cairo; the west end is our choice, not a source’s. The Shawnee moved their towns to the Scioto, Little Miami, Mad River and Great Miami valleys; Old Chillicothe near Xenia lasted 1774–80. The dashed counties are a town footprint, not a boundary. The 1786 Treaty of Fort Finney offered land “to live and hunt upon” in Ohio but describes it partly by an unlocated river, so it is not drawn.

eras.text: On 3 Aug 1795 the tribes at Greenville ceded most of Ohio and a strip of Indiana east and south of a line from the Cuyahoga mouth via Fort Loramie and Fort Recovery to the Ohio opposite the mouth of the Kentucky River. Article 7 allowed hunting on ceded land. The line follows the treaty’s calls; the hatched area is closed by hand along the Ohio River and Lake Erie. Greenville does not mention a Shawnee claim inside Kentucky, and the sources give no later date for it, so the Kentucky general area is shown only to 1795.

properties.note: Ohio River from the Kanawha mouth to Cairo, following Natural Earth centreline. The treaty terms are not preserved; sources say the Shawnee recognised the Ohio as boundary and would not hunt south of it. The west end (Cairo) is my choice, not a source call.

Counties containing Shawnee towns 1774-1795: Pickaway and Ross (Scioto Chillicothe/Camp Charlotte area), Greene (Old Chillicothe/Oldtown), Clark, Champaign and Logan (Mad River towns), Miami (Piqua, Great Miami), Auglaize and Allen (St. Marys, Wapakoneta area). Modern counties; presence footprint only.

Greenville, 3 Aug 1795, Art. 3: Cuyahoga mouth, Akron portage, Tuscarawas crossing (Bolivar), Loramie, Fort Recovery, then straight to the Ohio opposite the Kentucky River mouth. Vertices are modern town locations; the Tuscarawas and portage legs are simplified.
Land east and south of the Greenville line within Ohio and Indiana, closed by hand along the Ohio River and Lake Erie. Art. 7 kept hunting rights on ceded land.
